growth_story.headline: Since the 2001 crisis Türkiye's income per person has grown 4.3 percent a year, rising through repeated shocks and high inflation to a new peak in 2025.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2001 income per person grew only 1.8 percent a year: inflation never fell below 50 percent, peaking at 105.2 in 1994, and output fell sharply in 1994, 1999 and 2001 (-6.6). The World Bank credits the response to the 2001 crisis, a strict clean-up of the banks under independent supervisors and an independent central bank, with a regime shift, and from 2002 to 2025 growth averaged 4.3 percent a year as inflation dropped to 8.6 by 2004. The era held through the 2009 fall (-6.2) with fast rebounds in 2010 and 2011, though the World Bank wrote in 2014 that reform had slowed while cheap global money flowed in. From 2018 a currency crisis, the pandemic and unconventional policy from 2021 to 2023 made growth swing between -0.1 in 2019 and 10.8 in 2021, and inflation reached 72.3 percent in 2022. After monetary policy tightened from May 2023, inflation fell to 34.9 percent in 2025 while growth held at 3.1 in 2024 and 3.2 in 2025, taking income per person to its highest level yet, 15,883 dollars in constant prices. Growth over 2016–2025 averaged 3.7 percent a year, a little below the 3.9 of 2006–2015.

threads.title: Crisis and regime shift, 2001
threads.text: The 1990s brought high inflation and three deep falls in income per person, ending in the 2001 crisis. The World Bank credits the response, which took over failing banks while protecting depositors and relied on independent bank supervisors and an independent central bank, with a regime shift and an era of faster growth.

growth_story.tension: The IMF says productivity has stalled in recent years, yet income per person rose every year from 2020 to 2025, reached a new peak in 2025 and grew 3.7 percent a year over 2016–2025, well above the structural-peer median of 2.2. The sources trace recent growth mainly to strong spending, gold price gains and earthquake rebuilding rather than to gains in efficiency. The same IMF report notes that the authorities see it differently and say productivity has risen since the pandemic.
